sections.heading: Technique
lines: Supine MRI of the lumbar spine: sagittal T1 and T2; axial T2 at L3-L4, L4-L5, and L5-S1.

sections.heading: Findings
lines: L4-L5: grade I degenerative spondylolisthesis. Translation measures approximately 2.5 mm on this supine study.
L4-L5: a broad disc bulge, advanced facet hypertrophy, and ligamentum flavum thickening produce severe central and bilateral lateral-recess stenosis, right greater than left.
L4-L5: dural sac cross-sectional area approximately 58 mm².
L4-L5 facet joint effusions: right approximately 2.5 mm, left approximately 1.8 mm.
No synovial cyst. No dominant foraminal stenosis.
L3-L4: mild degeneration without clinically significant stenosis.
L5-S1: mild degeneration without clinically relevant stenosis.
No tumor, infection, or fracture.

sections.heading: Impression
lines: Severe multifactorial L4-L5 central and bilateral lateral-recess stenosis, right greater than left, with grade I degenerative spondylolisthesis (approximately 2.5 mm on supine imaging).
Mild, non-dominant degeneration at L3-L4 and L5-S1.

faculty_perspective.heading: Faculty perspective
faculty_perspective.intro: One experienced view of this case, offered for reflection. It is not an answer key, and thoughtful surgeons may reasonably differ.

sections.title: The clinical picture
sections.text: Elena's leg-dominant symptoms, provoked by standing and walking and relieved by flexion, describe neurogenic claudication. The subtle right EHL weakness and dorsal-foot sensory change point to the right L5 root. Present pulses and a negative straight-leg raise help keep vascular claudication and a disc herniation lower on the list. Much of the diagnosis is available before any imaging.

sections.title: Position matters
sections.text: Translation at L4-L5 was 4.5 mm standing, 6.0 mm in flexion, 3.0 mm in extension, and 2.5 mm on supine MRI. A supine study alone underestimates the slip under load. Facet effusions and the 8-degree angular change raise the question of instability, while the absent vacuum phenomenon and partially preserved disc height point the other way. No single threshold settles it.

sections.title: Decompression with or without fusion
sections.text: Reasonable surgeons disagree here, and the published trials have not converged. A useful question is what the decompression itself will do to stability, and how much the remaining motion matters for this patient. Her wish to avoid an extensive operation, her mild osteopenia and her preserved alignment all belong in that conversation. A clearly recorded threshold for later fusion is as important as the initial choice.

sections.title: Complementary tests
sections.text: The EMG and the earlier right L5 block are concordant with the clinical and imaging picture, but neither is definitive. They support a decision; they do not make it.

sections.title: The durotomy
sections.text: A recognized small defect is best repaired at once, with a watertight closure and a deliberate check before leaving the field. The more useful habit is to plan the postoperative watch at that moment: what you will ask nursing to report, and what would prompt imaging.

sections.title: Day 3
sections.text: Orthostatic headache with clear drainage after a known durotomy points strongly to a CSF leak. The task is to confirm it, exclude infection and a compressive collection, and choose a response proportionate to the findings. Observation, lumbar drainage and early re-exploration each have a place. They differ mainly in burden and in how quickly they settle the problem.

sections.title: Across the case
sections.text: Notice where your confidence moved, and whether new information or habit moved it. That is the most transferable lesson of a case like this.
